title: Pre-sales: selling the building before it exists
summary: A condominium is usually financed by selling units before construction, taking deposits from buyers, and showing a lender enough firm sales to prove the building will be bought. This lesson teaches deposit structures, trust and escrow, deposit insurance, pre-sale thresholds and what happens when a buyer walks away, and why the buyers' money is never the developer's to spend.
body:
Pre-sales turn a forecast into evidence. A buyer who signs a contract and pays a deposit tells the lender the building will sell, but that deposit is held for the buyer's protection, not the developer's convenience, and the whole structure works only if the money is kept where the law and the contract say.

Recall

Q. What is the in-balance test in a construction loan?

A. A check that the undrawn loan plus any committed equity is enough to pay every remaining cost to completion. If it is not, the borrower must put in the shortfall before the next draw.

Q. What is a condition precedent to the first draw?

A. Something that must be satisfied before the lender is obliged to make its first advance, such as the permit, the construction contract, a pre-leasing or pre-sale level, and the borrower's equity spent in full.

Q. How does a conditional purchase protect a buyer of land?

A. It lets the buyer sign a binding contract that only completes if stated conditions, such as financing, approvals or diligence, are satisfied by a date, so the buyer can walk away if they are not.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a rental building is financed on income. A condominium has no income: it is sold, unit by unit, and the sales are the repayment. Before a lender will fund the build, it wants proof that buyers exist at the prices in your pro forma. Pre-sales are that proof. They also bring in deposits, which in some places may be used for certain project costs and in others must sit untouched until the buyer takes title. Getting the deposit rules wrong is not a financing mistake; it can be a breach of trust and of consumer protection law. The rules differ by jurisdiction. Professional sign-off required: a real estate lawyer qualified where the project is built.

Deposit structures: how much, and when

A buyer signs a purchase agreement for a unit at a fixed price, to be completed when the building is finished and the unit can be registered as a separate title. The buyer pays a deposit, usually in stages: an amount at signing, another after any cooling-off period, and further amounts at set dates or construction milestones. The total deposit is often a meaningful share of the price. These percentages are commercial practice and, in some places, are capped or regulated by law; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

Here is the first worked example. A hypothetical 100-unit building has an average price of 500,000 dollars, total gross sales of 50,000,000. The deposit schedule is 5 percent at signing, 5 percent at 90 days and 5 percent at the start of the structure: 15 percent in total. If every unit sold, deposits would reach 0.15 multiplied by 50,000,000, which is 7,500,000 dollars. The balance of 85 percent, 42,500,000, arrives only at completion, usually from the buyers' own mortgages. That balance is what repays the construction loan, which is why the lender cares so much about whether each buyer will actually close.

Trust, escrow and deposit insurance

Deposits are normally held by a third party: a lawyer's trust account, an escrow agent or a regulated trustee. A deposit trust means the money belongs to the buyer until completion, held under rules that say when, and only when, it may be released. In some systems deposits stay in trust until the buyer takes title. In others they may be released to the developer for construction costs if the deposits are protected by deposit insurance or a bond, a policy from an insurer or a guarantee from a surety that repays buyers if the project fails. The insurer charges a premium and usually requires its own security and indemnities from the developer.

The professional framing is simple: until the law and the contract allow release, deposits are not a source of funds. They do not reduce your equity, and they do not pay a contractor. Where release is allowed, the released amount becomes a liability owed back to the buyer if the sale fails, so it sits on your sources and uses as borrowed money with conditions, not as revenue.

Say that out loud now.

Pre-sale thresholds: what the lender counts

A pre-sale threshold is the level of firm sales a construction lender requires before the first draw. It is usually expressed as a percentage of units or of sales value, or as a coverage test: the net proceeds from qualifying sales must cover the loan, or a stated multiple of it. The thresholds are commercial practice set by each lender, not standards.

The second worked example. The lender requires qualifying pre-sales whose net proceeds cover 100 percent of the 35,000,000 dollar loan. You have 72 signed contracts with a total price of 36,000,000. The lender excludes three contracts signed by a company related to you, worth 1,500,000, and two still within their cooling-off period, worth 1,000,000. Qualifying sales are 36,000,000 minus 2,500,000, which is 33,500,000. Net proceeds after deducting, say, 4 percent for commissions and closing costs are 0.96 multiplied by 33,500,000, about 32,160,000. That is short of the 35,000,000 loan by about 2,840,000. You need roughly six more qualifying sales at the average price, or a smaller loan, before the first draw.

When a buyer walks away

Some buyers will not close: their mortgage is refused, prices have fallen below their contract, or their circumstances change. A buyer who fails to complete is in default under the purchase agreement. The developer's remedy depends on the contract and the law: often keeping all or part of the deposit, possibly claiming damages if the unit resells for less, and reselling the unit. In a rising market this is a small problem. In a falling market it is the central risk of the whole project, because the deposits are a fraction of the price and the loan is repaid from closings, not deposits.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is treating buyers' deposits as the developer's money, spending them where the law does not allow or relying on them to fund a project that is otherwise short of equity. The control is a written deposit protocol from your lawyer stating where every deposit is held, when it may be released and against what protection, reconciled monthly against the trust account statements.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner counts every signed contract towards the pre-sale threshold. Lenders count qualifying sales only: arm's length buyers, outside any cooling-off period, with the required deposit paid and no unusual conditions.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: the timing of revenue recognition and any transaction tax on a new unit can follow completion rather than deposit receipt; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: mishandling trust money can expose the developer and its directors personally. Banking: the lender will usually take security over the purchase agreements and require pre-sale coverage as a condition to the first draw. Governance: the board should approve the deposit protocol and receive a monthly trust reconciliation. Estate: a project company's obligations to buyers continue regardless of what happens to its owner, so continuity of signing authority matters. Exit: the developer's profit arrives only at closing, and buyer defaults at completion can turn that profit into a shortfall.

Callback

In week 28 we turned absorption into a number. Pre-sales are absorption measured before the building exists, and the lender's threshold is simply the absorption it must see before it will take construction risk. A feasibility study that predicted the sales pace is now tested against signed contracts.

Recap

Deposits arrive in stages and belong to the buyer until the law and the contract allow release. Trust, escrow and insurance protect them. Lenders count qualifying sales only, and test net proceeds against the loan. Buyer default is the central risk in a falling market.

Next: Ford, with Roman, takes Evergrande through failure forensics: a pre-sale model that turned buyers' money into working capital.
checklist: Write the deposit schedule as amounts and dates for every unit
Obtain a written deposit protocol from a lawyer where the project is built
Confirm where deposits are held and when they may be released
Price any deposit insurance or bond and its security demands
List the lender's definition of a qualifying sale
Calculate net proceeds of qualifying sales against the loan
Stress closings for buyer default in a falling market
Reconcile the trust account monthly and report to the board
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, pre-sales in one minute. A condominium is repaid by closings, not income, so the lender wants proof that buyers exist before it funds the build. Buyers sign at a fixed price and pay deposits in stages, perhaps 15 percent in total, with the balance at completion. Deposits belong to the buyer until the law and the contract allow release, and are held in trust or escrow; in some places they may be released for construction if they are insured. The lender sets a pre-sale threshold and counts qualifying sales only. On 72 contracts worth 36,000,000, removing related-party and cooling-off sales leaves 33,500,000, about 32,160,000 after costs, short of a 35,000,000 loan. When buyers walk away in a falling market, the deposit covers only part of the loss. Buyers' money is never my working capital.
terms: Pre-sale threshold — the level of firm, qualifying sales a construction lender requires before it will fund a condominium build.
Deposit trust — an arrangement under which a buyer's deposit is held by a third party for the buyer until completion or a permitted release.
Deposit insurance — a policy or bond that repays buyers' deposits if the project fails, often allowing deposits to be released for construction where the law permits.

hostile.q: You say you have 72 pre-sales. How many of them will we actually count?
hostile.a: Sixty-seven. I have excluded three contracts signed by a related company and two still in their cooling-off period. On the remaining 33,500,000, net proceeds after commissions and closing costs are about 32,160,000, which is about 2,840,000 short of your loan. I will either sell about six more units or reduce the loan, and I will show you the qualifying list each month.

title: Evergrande: when buyers' money became working capital
summary: China Evergrande grew into one of the country's largest developers on a model that relied heavily on pre-sales and borrowing, then defaulted on its offshore debt in 2021 and was ordered into liquidation by a Hong Kong court in 2024. Ford, with Roman, takes the case through seven steps and finds the root cause in completing sold homes with money from the next sale.
rule: Rule 41: Buyers' deposits are never my working capital; they stay in trust or are released only against protection the law allows, and every build must be fully funded without any deposit I could be forced to return.
body:
Evergrande did not fail because people stopped wanting homes. It failed because the homes it had already sold were being finished with money from homes it had not yet built, and the moment new sales and new loans slowed, the unfinished buildings had no money behind them.

Recall

Q. What is a pre-sale threshold?

A. The level of firm, qualifying sales a construction lender requires before it will fund a condominium build.

Q. What is a lender's monitor, in construction lending?

A. An independent professional who reviews the budget, schedule and work in place for the lender, and certifies each draw.

Q. What was the root cause in the Dubai World case?

A. A maturity mismatch: long developments funded with shorter debt that depended on refinancing, rising prices and support that was never written down.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the outline below is the broad public record; verify dates and details against reliable sources before you rely on them, and treat any figure you meet elsewhere as needing confirmation. The scale is enormous, but the mechanism is the same one a small developer can reproduce with two projects and a shared bank account. Roman assists, because the case sits where pre-sale finance meets the lender's view of risk.

Step 1: the timeline

Evergrande was founded in the 1990s and grew over two decades into one of China's largest property developers, building and selling homes across many cities and expanding into businesses far beyond property. Much of its growth was funded by selling homes before completion and by borrowing from banks, bond investors and other sources, including investment products sold to individuals. In August 2020, Chinese authorities introduced limits on developers' leverage, widely known as the "three red lines", which restricted further borrowing by developers that breached them. Through 2021 Evergrande's liquidity worsened; it struggled to pay suppliers and investors, and in late 2021 it missed payments on its offshore bonds and was declared in default by rating agencies. During 2022 many homebuyers across China whose homes were unfinished, at Evergrande and other developers, publicly refused to keep paying their mortgages. In January 2024 a Hong Kong court ordered the company to be liquidated.

Step 2: the key decisions

Three decisions mattered most. Growing by launching new projects funded largely by pre-sales of those projects and of others. Pooling cash across the group so that money received for one project could be spent on another. And diversifying into unrelated businesses with borrowed money while the core business depended on continued sales.

Step 3: the assumptions

The model assumed sales would keep growing, that prices would keep rising so that every launch sold quickly, and that lenders would keep lending. It assumed, in effect, that the business could always sell tomorrow's homes to finish today's. When credit was restricted and buyers hesitated, every assumption failed at once, because they were all the same assumption: that the cycle would not turn.

Say that out loud now.

Step 4: the incentives

Fast launches brought in deposits and down payments that funded growth, so the company was rewarded for selling more and building later. Buyers were rewarded, while prices rose, for buying early at a discount. Local governments earned revenue from land sales. Lenders and investors earned returns on a borrower that seemed too large to fail. Hardly anyone in the chain was rewarded for insisting that each project's money stay with that project.

Step 5: the warning signs ignored

Growing debts alongside growing unsold inventory. Payments to suppliers stretched and sometimes made with promissory notes rather than cash. Investment products sold to individuals and staff to raise money. A regulatory change aimed specifically at developer leverage. Each was public, and each pointed to a company whose cash depended on raising more.

Step 6: the point of no return

The point of no return was the moment new sales and new borrowing could no longer cover the cost of finishing homes already sold. After that, every unfinished project competed for the same shrinking pool of cash, and buyers who had paid were left waiting for homes that the company could not afford to complete.

Step 7: the root cause

The root cause was using buyers' money as working capital: cash received for specific homes funded other projects and other businesses, so completing the sold homes depended on selling more. Roman's lender view: a pre-sale is only as good as the separation between the buyer's money and the developer's other needs. Where that separation exists by law and by practice, a slowdown delays a developer. Where it does not, a slowdown can strand thousands of buyers.

The same mechanism, at small scale

This is a composite example. A developer has two hypothetical condominium projects. Project A has 6,000,000 dollars of deposits released under insurance. Project B is short of equity by 2,000,000. In a jurisdiction where released deposits may only be used on the project that raised them, using 2,000,000 of Project A's released deposits on Project B is almost certainly a breach of the insurer's terms and the deposit rules. In any jurisdiction it moves Project A's completion risk onto Project B's sales. If Project B's sales stall, Project A cannot finish, its buyers are owed their deposits, and the insurer pursues the developer's indemnity. The arithmetic is simple: Project A now needs 2,000,000 that is not there.

The second worked example measures dependency. Suppose a developer's plan shows completion of Project A funded 70 percent by its construction loan, 15 percent by equity and 15 percent by released deposits. If deposits had to be returned or held back, the funding gap is 15 percent of cost. Rule 41 asks you to show that gap could be met without new sales: from committed equity, an undrawn loan facility, or a guarantee from someone with assets. If it cannot, the project is depending on buyers' money it may not keep.

What a buyer, an insurer and a lender would check

Each party who depends on your deposits can run the same three checks. Is each project in its own company with its own bank account? Does the deposit ledger reconcile to the trust account statement every month, to the dollar? And does the funding plan show the project completing if no deposit were ever released? A developer who can answer all three on one page, before being asked, removes the single question that sank Evergrande's buyers: whether the money they paid for their home was still there.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is pooling project cash so that one project's buyers fund another's shortfall. The control is a separate company, bank account and deposit ledger for every project, with any transfer between projects approved in writing by the lender and the deposit insurer.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner sees released deposits sitting in an account and treats them as free cash for the most urgent need. They are a liability owed back to buyers if the sale fails.

The prevention rule

Rule 41: Buyers' deposits are never my working capital; they stay in trust or are released only against protection the law allows, and every build must be fully funded without any deposit I could be forced to return.

Callback

In week 35 we learned to put each project in its own entity with its own minute book and signing authority. Evergrande shows why that separation must extend to money. A separate company is little protection if cash flows freely between projects; the bank account and the deposit ledger must be as separate as the share register.

Recap

A pre-sale model became a growth engine fuelled by buyers' money and borrowing. When credit was restricted and sales slowed, sold homes could not be finished. The root cause was buyers' money used as working capital. Keep each project's money in its own ledger and fund every build without depending on deposits you might have to return.

Next: Sage on the money: how pre-sales change the capital stack, the price you sell at, and your return.
checklist: Keep a separate company, bank account and deposit ledger for each project
Forbid transfers between projects without lender and insurer approval
Show how the build is funded if released deposits had to be returned
Treat released deposits as a liability on sources and uses
Monitor supplier payment terms for stretching as a warning sign
Review sales pace against new launches every month
Never fund a new launch from an existing project's buyers
State Rule 41 before releasing any deposit
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, Evergrande in one minute. Evergrande grew into one of China's largest developers by selling homes before completion and borrowing heavily, while diversifying far beyond property. Cash from one project's buyers funded other projects and businesses. In 2020 Chinese authorities limited developer borrowing; in 2021 Evergrande missed offshore bond payments and was declared in default; in 2022 many buyers of unfinished homes across China refused to keep paying their mortgages; and in January 2024 a Hong Kong court ordered liquidation. The root cause was using buyers' money as working capital, so finishing sold homes depended on selling more. At small scale, moving one project's released deposits to another moves the completion risk with them. Rule 41: buyers' deposits are never my working capital, and every build must be fully funded without any deposit I could be forced to return.
terms: Working capital — the cash a business uses to fund its day-to-day operations and short-term obligations.
Pooling — combining cash from separate projects or entities into one account so that it can be spent wherever needed.
Liquidation — the court-supervised winding up of a company, in which its assets are realised and distributed to creditors.

hostile.q: Your two projects share a treasury account. How do I know Project A's deposits are not funding Project B?
hostile.a: They cannot, by structure. Each project is a separate company with its own bank account and deposit ledger, deposits are held in a lawyer's trust account, and released deposits on Project A may be spent only on Project A's certified costs under the insurer's terms. I will give you the monthly trust reconciliation and the bank statements for both companies, and no inter-project transfer happens without your written consent.

title: How pre-sales change the money: price, pace and the capital stack
summary: Pre-sales do three things to the money: they unlock the construction loan, they may reduce equity if deposits can be released, and they fix prices years before completion. This lesson puts numbers on each, adds Warrick's Wealth Ledger on when a condominium profit is really yours, and opens the monthly thread on ethics and anti-corruption.
body:
Every pre-sale is a trade. You give up the price the unit might fetch at completion in exchange for certainty today: a loan you could not otherwise get, and sometimes cash you could not otherwise use. Price that trade explicitly, because it is the biggest pricing decision in a condominium.

Recall

Q. What was the root cause in the Evergrande case?

A. Using buyers' money as working capital, so that completing homes already sold depended on selling more.

Q. What does a completion guarantee promise a construction lender?

A. That the guarantor will cause the project to be finished, or pay the cost of finishing it, if the borrower cannot.

Q. How do you value land contributed by a landowner to a joint venture?

A. Agree a value in advance, usually by appraisal or by residual land value, and record it as that partner's capital contribution, so later profit sharing rests on an agreed number.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a condominium's return depends less on construction cost than on two decisions: how fast you sell, and at what price. Pre-sales fix both before you have built anything. Sell too cheaply and you have given away the profit to early buyers. Sell too slowly and you have no loan. All figures here are hypothetical, and deposit release rules depend on the jurisdiction.

Pre-sales unlock the loan

A construction lender will not fund a condominium on forecast sales alone. Pre-sales reduce its risk because they show the exit, so they decide the loan amount and the start date. Some lenders also scale the loan to the strength of the sales: more qualifying sales, a higher loan-to-cost. That makes the pre-sale pace a financing variable, not only a marketing one.

The first worked example. A hypothetical project costs 40,000,000 dollars and has gross sales value of 50,000,000. One lender offers 65 percent loan-to-cost, 26,000,000, at 60 percent pre-sales by value. Another offers 75 percent, 30,000,000, at 80 percent pre-sales. The second loan saves 4,000,000 of equity but requires 10,000,000 more of qualifying sales before the first draw. If reaching 80 percent takes six more months and each month costs, say, 150,000 in land carry and overheads, the delay costs about 900,000. And if you discount prices to sell faster, the true cost is the discount plus the carry. The larger loan is not automatically the better one.

Deposits as a source of funds

Where the law allows deposits to be released for construction against insurance, they can replace some equity. In the same example, suppose deposits of 15 percent on 40,000,000 of qualifying sales, 6,000,000, may be released after insurance. If the lender allows them to be spent before its own funds, equity might fall from 14,000,000 to 8,000,000. Equity of 8,000,000 earning the same 10,000,000 profit is a far higher multiple than 14,000,000 earning it.

But price the cost. The insurer charges a premium and usually takes an indemnity from the developer and often from you personally. The released deposits must be repaid if sales fail. So the true structure is: equity of 8,000,000, plus 6,000,000 of buyer money that behaves like a conditional loan, backed by your indemnity. If you would not sign a personal guarantee for 6,000,000 of debt, you should hesitate to sign an indemnity that has the same effect.

Say that out loud now.

Price against pace

The second worked example is the pricing trade. You plan to sell 100 units at an average of 500,000 dollars. If you price the first 40 units at a 5 percent launch discount, 475,000, you give up 25,000 a unit, or 1,000,000 dollars. In exchange, you might reach the lender's threshold four months sooner, saving 600,000 in carry, and start construction before a forecast rise in building costs. Whether 1,000,000 of discount is worth 600,000 of carry plus an earlier start depends on how sure you are of the cost rise and of the later prices. The professional habit is to write that trade down, with its numbers, before setting the launch price.

Remember too that a pre-sale fixes price for years. If prices rise 10 percent by completion, the buyer captures that gain, not you. If prices fall 10 percent, many buyers will try not to close. Pre-sales give away much of the upside and keep much of the downside risk with you. That asymmetry is why the deposit size and the buyer default remedy matter so much.

How the best do it

Experienced condominium developers commonly release inventory in phases rather than all at once, raising prices between phases as sales evidence builds, so early discounts apply only to the units needed to reach the lender's threshold. They price each phase against current absorption data rather than the original pro forma. And they keep a minimum share of the best units unsold until later, where the price evidence will be strongest. A small developer can copy all three with a phased price list approved before launch.

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's view of your personal balance sheet. A condominium's profit is not yours when the units are pre-sold, nor when the building tops out. It becomes yours only after closings have repaid the loan, every buyer default is resolved, any warranty obligations are provided for, and the indemnities to insurers are released. Until then, record your interest at cost, not at forecast profit, and list every indemnity and guarantee as a contingent liability at its full amount. A licensed adviser is required before you act.

Ethics and anti-corruption

This month's thread is ethics. Deposits are other people's savings held for a purpose. The temptation to use them, even briefly, even with every intention of putting them back, is exactly how small breaches become large ones. The rule is simple and absolute: trust money moves only as the protocol allows.

The same applies to anyone who controls a step you need: an official who could speed an approval, a lender's staff member who could overlook a sale that does not qualify. Never offer, and never accept, anything to influence those decisions, and keep a written record of every gift or hospitality offered to you. Corruption laws differ by jurisdiction and can reach conduct abroad; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

A note on the upside you give away

Run the pricing trade one step further. If 80 units are pre-sold at an average of 490,000 and prices rise 8 percent by completion, the units would have fetched about 529,200 each, so about 39,200 a unit, or roughly 3,136,000 in total, has passed to buyers. That is the real cost of certainty. It is often worth paying, because without pre-sales there is no loan; but it belongs on the decision memo, not only in hindsight.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is discounting the launch price to reach a pre-sale threshold faster without measuring what the discount costs against what the speed saves. The control is a written price-against-pace calculation, approved before the price list is published.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner treats released deposits as equity. They are buyers' money backed by an indemnity, and they come back as a liability if sales fail.

Callback

In week 37 we learned that each layer of the capital stack has a position and a price. Released deposits are a layer too: they sit, in effect, beside the senior loan, are owed back to buyers if the project fails, and are backed by your indemnity to the insurer. Draw them on the stack before you count them as funding.

Recap

Pre-sales unlock and size the loan, can replace some equity where deposits may be released, and fix prices years ahead. Price the discount against the carry saved, release inventory in phases, record profit only after closings, and never move trust money outside the protocol.

Next: LEX on the rules: trust accounts, disclosure, cooling-off rights and buyer default, and how Canada and Guyana approach off-plan sales.
checklist: Compare loan offers by pre-sale requirement and the time it costs
Price any launch discount against the carry it saves
Treat released deposits as a conditional liability, not equity
List every insurer indemnity as a contingent liability
Release inventory in phases with an approved price list
Hold back a share of the best units for later phases
Record condominium profit only after closings and releases
Never move trust money outside the written protocol
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, the money in pre-sales in one minute. Pre-sales unlock and size the construction loan, so sales pace is a financing variable. A larger loan that needs more pre-sales may cost more in carry and discounts than it saves in equity. Where deposits may be released against insurance, they can replace equity, but they remain buyers' money, owed back if sales fail and backed by my indemnity, so I treat them as a conditional loan. A 5 percent discount on 40 units costs 1,000,000; it is worth it only if the speed saves more. Pre-sales give buyers much of the upside and leave much of the downside with me. The best developers release inventory in phases and raise prices as evidence builds. On my own balance sheet, the profit is mine only after closings repay the loan and every indemnity is released.
terms: Launch discount — a price reduction offered to early buyers to accelerate pre-sales.
Phased release — selling a project's units in stages, adjusting prices between stages as sales evidence builds.
Indemnity — a promise to compensate another party, such as a deposit insurer, for losses it suffers.

hostile.q: Why should we accept your deposits as part of the funding when you could be forced to return them?
hostile.a: You should not count them as equity, and I do not. The build is fully funded by your loan and our equity, with released deposits used only to reduce interest, spent only on certified costs of this project under the insurer's terms. If every deposit had to be returned, our committed equity and a standby guarantee cover the gap, and I will show you that calculation.

title: The rules of off-plan sales: trust, disclosure, cooling-off and default
summary: Selling homes before they exist is closely regulated in many places, because buyers hand over savings years before receiving anything. This lesson teaches how deposit trust rules, disclosure obligations, cooling-off rights and buyer default remedies work in concept, and compares how Canada and Guyana approach off-plan sales.
body:
An off-plan purchase agreement is a consumer contract with a long gap between payment and delivery, so the law often steps in on the buyer's side. Know which rules protect the buyer's money, what you must disclose, when a buyer may walk away for free, and what you may keep when a buyer walks away in breach.

Recall

Q. What is a launch discount, and when is it worth giving?

A. A reduced price for early buyers to accelerate pre-sales. It is worth giving only if the carry and cost savings from reaching the lender's threshold sooner exceed the revenue given up.

Q. What is a carve-out in a non-recourse loan?

A. A listed exception, such as fraud, misappropriation of funds or environmental loss, for which the guarantor becomes personally liable even though the loan is otherwise non-recourse.

Q. What does a non-disclosure agreement in a land deal protect?

A. Confidential information shared during negotiations, such as the seller's data or the buyer's plans, by limiting who may see it and what it may be used for.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, mishandling a buyer's deposit can be a breach of trust, a consumer protection offence and a loan default at once, and notice the carve-out in today's recall: misappropriation of funds is one of the classic items that converts a non-recourse loan into personal liability. What follows teaches concepts, not any jurisdiction's law. Professional sign-off required: a real estate lawyer qualified where the project is built and, if you sell to buyers abroad, advice on the law where they live.

Trust rules: whose money it is

In many systems, deposits on new homes must be paid to a lawyer, licensed broker, escrow agent or trustee, and held in a designated trust account. The rules typically say what the trustee may do with the money, whether interest is earned and for whom, and when the money may be released: on completion and registration of the buyer's title, or earlier against insurance or a bond if the law allows. A trustee who releases money outside the rules can be personally liable, and so can a developer who directs the release. The professional point is that the trust rules override the purchase agreement: a clause letting you use deposits does not help if the statute forbids it.

Disclosure: what the buyer must be told

Many jurisdictions require a developer to give buyers a disclosure statement before or at signing: a document describing the project, the unit, the budget for the condominium corporation, the declaration and bylaws, any known risks, the expected completion date and how deposits are protected. Material changes to that information may have to be disclosed later, and in some places a material change gives the buyer a right to cancel. The drafting lesson for a developer is to describe the project accurately and conservatively. An optimistic completion date or an understated common expense budget is not marketing; it can become a ground for cancellation or a claim.

Say that out loud now.

Cooling-off rights

A rescission period, often called a cooling-off period, is a short window after signing during which a buyer may cancel the purchase without penalty and recover the deposit. Its length, and whether it exists at all, depends on the jurisdiction; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. This is why lenders exclude sales still inside the rescission period from qualifying pre-sales: the buyer can walk away for free.

The first worked example. A developer signs 20 contracts in a launch weekend, each with a 10-day rescission period in this hypothetical. The sales report on day 5 shows 20 sales. On day 11 it shows 17, because three buyers rescinded. Any decision made on day 5, such as ordering materials or reporting 20 sales to the lender, was made on numbers that were legally provisional. The control is to report sales in two columns, firm and within rescission, until the period ends.

Buyer default: what you may keep

When a buyer fails to complete, the purchase agreement usually lets the developer terminate, keep the deposit and resell the unit, and sometimes claim the shortfall on resale as damages. Courts in many common law jurisdictions have historically been willing to let a seller keep a reasonable deposit on a buyer's default, while being more cautious about amounts that look like a penalty rather than a genuine deposit or pre-estimate of loss. Where that line falls, and whether a statute caps forfeiture, depends on the jurisdiction and the wording.

The second worked example. A buyer contracted at 500,000 dollars and paid a 15 percent deposit, 75,000. At completion, the market has fallen and the buyer does not close. The unit resells for 450,000, with resale costs of 20,000. The developer's loss is 500,000 minus 450,000 plus 20,000, which is 70,000. If the contract and the law allow the developer to keep the deposit as against its loss, the 75,000 roughly covers it. If prices had fallen to 400,000, the loss would be 120,000 and the deposit would cover only part; recovering the rest means pursuing the buyer, who may have no assets in your jurisdiction.

Sunset and termination clauses

Many purchase agreements let either side terminate if the project is not completed by an outside date, often called a sunset clause, with deposits refunded. In a rising market a developer might be tempted to delay and terminate in order to resell at higher prices; several jurisdictions have legislated against that practice. Draft sunset dates realistically and never treat them as an option to reprice.

Two Systems

A conceptual comparison only; verify against primary source for both countries before relying on it. In Canada, consumer protection, real estate marketing and condominium law are largely provincial, so the rules on where deposits are held, whether they may be released, deposit protection schemes, disclosure statements and rescission periods differ from province to province. A developer selling in one province cannot assume another's rules. Guyana has its own legislation on land, conveyancing and companies, and the questions to put to counsel there are whether a specific statute governs off-plan sales and deposits, whether a strata or condominium title regime exists that allows individual units to be registered separately, who may hold deposits and under what trust rules, and whether consumer protection law gives buyers a cooling-off right. Where buyers live abroad, as diaspora buyers often do, the law of the buyer's country may also affect marketing and enforcement. The concept is the same in both places: the buyer's protection is set by statute and trust law, not only by your contract.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is relying on a clause in your purchase agreement that the governing statute overrides, especially on deposit use or forfeiture. The control is a legal opinion, before launch, confirming that the agreement, the disclosure statement and the deposit protocol comply with the law where the project is built.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner reports sales inside the rescission period as firm. They are provisional until the period ends, and the lender will not count them.

Callback

In week 30 we read condominium declarations: the registered document that creates the units and common elements. The disclosure statement is the buyer's first view of that declaration, years before it is registered. If the declaration changes materially between the two, the buyer may gain a right to walk away, so keep them aligned from the first draft.

Recap

Deposits are held in trust under rules the contract cannot override. Disclose accurately and conservatively. Report rescission-period sales separately. Expect to keep a reasonable deposit on buyer default, not a penalty. Set realistic sunset dates. And confirm all of it with counsel where the project is built.

Next: Priya with the numbers: testing pre-sale coverage, deposits and buyer defaults step by step.
checklist: Confirm where deposits must be held and when they may be released
Obtain a legal opinion on the agreement, disclosure and deposit protocol
Prepare a conservative disclosure statement and track material changes
Report firm sales and rescission-period sales in separate columns
Check whether forfeiture of the deposit is capped or restricted
Set realistic sunset dates and never use them to reprice
Take advice on the buyer's home law for sales abroad
Professional sign-off required: real estate lawyer where the project is built
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, the rules of off-plan sales in one minute. Deposits are usually held in a trust account under rules that the purchase agreement cannot override, and releasing them outside those rules can make the trustee and the developer personally liable. Many places require a disclosure statement describing the project, the budget and how deposits are protected, and a material change can let a buyer cancel. A rescission period lets a buyer cancel for free, so sales inside it are provisional and lenders do not count them. When a buyer defaults, the developer can usually keep a reasonable deposit and resell; on a 500,000 sale with 75,000 deposited, a resale at 450,000 roughly covers the loss, but a resale at 400,000 does not. Sunset clauses must be realistic. Rules differ by province in Canada and have their own path in Guyana, so counsel confirms both.
terms: Disclosure statement — a document a developer gives a buyer describing the project, unit, budget, risks and deposit protection.
Rescission period — a short period after signing during which a buyer may cancel a purchase without penalty.
Forfeiture — the loss of a deposit by a buyer who fails to complete, subject to the contract and any legal limits.

hostile.q: Your agreement says you may use deposits for construction. Is that enough?
hostile.a: No. The trust rules where the project is built decide when deposits may be released, and the contract cannot override them. Before launch I will have a legal opinion confirming that release is permitted only against deposit insurance, only for this project's certified costs, and only after the rescission period, and our lawyer will hold every deposit until those conditions are met.

title: Testing pre-sale coverage, deposits and defaults, step by step
summary: A worked calculation takes a hypothetical condominium from its sales report to the lender's pre-sale test: filtering contracts to qualifying sales, calculating net proceeds against the loan, tracking deposits held, and stressing closings for buyer default at completion. Units are stated at every step.
body:
A sales report is a marketing document until you run it through the lender's definitions. Filter it to qualifying sales, convert price to net proceeds, and stress the closings, and you will know whether the project can draw its loan and repay it.

Recall

Q. Why are sales inside the rescission period excluded from qualifying pre-sales?

A. Because the buyer can still cancel without penalty, so the sale is provisional.

Q. What does the in-balance test require before each draw?

A. That the undrawn loan plus committed equity is enough to pay every remaining cost to completion.

Q. What does an option to purchase land give the developer?

A. The right, but not the obligation, to buy the land at a stated price within a stated period, in exchange for an option fee.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, the lender's credit team will run exactly these steps before the first draw and again before releasing the loan in full. Running them yourself, monthly, tells you how many more sales you need, at what price, and how much buyer default the project can absorb. All figures are hypothetical, and the lender's definitions are commercial practice that varies, not a standard.

Step 1: the project

A hypothetical condominium has 120 units at an average list price of 450,000 dollars: gross sales value of 120 multiplied by 450,000, which is 54,000,000 dollars. Total project cost is 42,000,000. The construction loan is 30,000,000. The lender's condition to first draw: net proceeds of qualifying pre-sales must be at least 110 percent of the loan, which is 1.10 multiplied by 30,000,000, or 33,000,000 dollars. Deposits are 15 percent of price, paid in three equal stages.

Step 2: the sales report

The report shows 92 signed contracts with a total price of 41,400,000 dollars. Now apply the lender's definition of a qualifying sale: arm's length buyer, outside the rescission period, first two deposit stages paid, no unusual conditions such as a financing condition or a right to assign before completion.

Remove 4 contracts signed by a company related to the developer: 1,800,000. Remove 6 contracts still within the rescission period: 2,700,000. Remove 3 contracts where the second deposit stage is overdue: 1,350,000. Remove 2 contracts containing a financing condition: 900,000. Total removed: 15 contracts and 6,750,000 dollars. Qualifying sales: 77 contracts and 41,400,000 minus 6,750,000, which is 34,650,000 dollars.

Step 3: net proceeds

The lender tests net proceeds, not price. Deduct sales commissions of, say, 4 percent and closing costs and transaction taxes borne by the developer of, say, 2 percent: 6 percent in total. Net proceeds are 0.94 multiplied by 34,650,000, which is 32,571,000 dollars. The requirement is 33,000,000. The shortfall is 33,000,000 minus 32,571,000, which is 429,000 dollars of net proceeds.

Convert that into units. Each additional average sale nets 0.94 multiplied by 450,000, which is 423,000 dollars. The shortfall of 429,000 needs about 1.01 sales, so two more qualifying sales, because you cannot sell part of a unit. Alternatively, the 6 rescission-period contracts will qualify automatically in a few days if none is cancelled, adding up to about 2,538,000 of net proceeds. The honest forecast is that the threshold will be met within the rescission period, provided at least two of the six buyers hold.

Say that out loud now.

Step 4: deposits held

On the 77 qualifying contracts, two of three deposit stages are paid: 10 percent of 34,650,000, which is 3,465,000 dollars, held in trust. The third stage, a further 1,732,500, falls due at the start of the structure. Your deposit ledger must reconcile to the trust account statement to the dollar. If it does not, find the difference before the lender's counsel does.

Step 5: stressing closings for buyer default

Now look forward to completion, when the loan is repaid from closings. Assume all 120 units are eventually sold at an average of 450,000. Suppose a falling market causes 10 percent of buyers, 12 units, to fail to close. Each defaulting buyer forfeits a 15 percent deposit of 67,500, so 12 units forfeit 810,000. The 12 units are resold at a hypothetical 10 percent below contract, 405,000 each, with resale costs of 4 percent. Resale net proceeds: 405,000 multiplied by 0.96 is 388,800 a unit, or 4,665,600 for twelve. Had those buyers closed, net proceeds would have been 450,000 multiplied by 0.94, or 423,000 each, 5,076,000 for twelve. The gap is 5,076,000 minus 4,665,600, which is 410,400, offset by the forfeited deposits of 810,000. In this case the deposits more than cover the loss.

Now the severe case: 25 percent default, 30 units, and resale at 20 percent below contract, 360,000. Forfeited deposits: 30 multiplied by 67,500 is 2,025,000. Resale net: 360,000 multiplied by 0.96 is 345,600 each, 10,368,000 for thirty, against 12,690,000 had they closed. The gap is 2,322,000, more than the deposits by 297,000. And the resales take time, during which interest runs. The lesson is not the exact number but the shape: deposits cushion moderate defaults and fail in severe ones.

Step 6: loan repayment

In the severe case, total net proceeds at completion would be about 54,000,000 multiplied by 0.94, which is 50,760,000, less the 2,322,000 gap, plus the 2,025,000 forfeited, about 50,463,000, received over a longer period. The 30,000,000 loan is still repaid, so the lender is safe; the developer's margin absorbs the loss and the delay. That is exactly why the lender sets a coverage test above 100 percent: the cushion protects it, and your equity takes the hit.

Step 7: what the numbers tell you to do

Turn the results into actions. Before the first draw, the gap is timing, not demand: watch the six rescission contracts and chase the overdue deposits, and do not discount prices to win two sales you are likely to get anyway. At completion, the severe case is the one to plan for, because it is the one the deposits do not cover. Three controls follow from the arithmetic. Keep the deposit percentage high enough that a moderate fall is fully covered; here 15 percent covered a 10 percent fall, but 10 percent would not have. Hold a contingency in equity or an undrawn facility at least equal to the severe-case gap, here about 300,000 plus the interest on the slower resales. And start a closing readiness programme six months before completion: confirm that each buyer has mortgage approval, so you learn about likely defaults while you still have time to remarket the units.

The second worked example in this step checks interest during resale. If 30 units take six months to resell and the loan balance still outstanding against them is, say, 8,000,000 at a hypothetical 8 percent, the extra interest is 8,000,000 multiplied by 0.08 multiplied by 0.5, or 320,000 dollars, which must be added to the severe-case gap.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is planning the first draw on the gross sales report rather than on qualifying net proceeds. The control is a monthly qualifying-sales schedule, built on the lender's definitions, with the shortfall stated in dollars and in units.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner assumes deposits will always cover a defaulting buyer's loss. They cover moderate falls; a severe fall with many defaults can exceed them, and the excess comes out of the developer's margin.

Callback

In week 14 we built revenue and absorption into the pro forma. Today's calculation tests that revenue line from the other end: not what you hope to sell, but what the lender will count, net of costs and stressed for buyers who do not close.

Recap

Filter the sales report to qualifying contracts, convert price to net proceeds, compare with the coverage requirement in dollars and units, reconcile deposits to the trust account, and stress closings for moderate and severe default. Deposits cushion a dip, not a crash.

Next: Priya in the room: the meeting where the lender says some of your sales do not count.
checklist: Calculate gross sales value and the lender's coverage requirement
Remove related-party, rescission, overdue-deposit and conditional contracts
Convert qualifying price to net proceeds after commissions and closing costs
State the shortfall in dollars and in units
Reconcile the deposit ledger to the trust account to the dollar
Stress closings at moderate and severe buyer default
Compare forfeited deposits with the resale gap in each case
Repeat the test monthly until the first draw
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, testing pre-sales in one minute. A 120-unit building at 450,000 dollars a unit has gross sales of 54,000,000. The lender needs net qualifying proceeds of 110 percent of a 30,000,000 loan, which is 33,000,000. The sales report shows 92 contracts worth 41,400,000. Removing related-party, rescission-period, overdue-deposit and conditional contracts leaves 77 worth 34,650,000. After 6 percent of costs, net proceeds are 32,571,000: 429,000 short, about two more sales. Deposits held are 3,465,000 and must match the trust account. At completion, if 10 percent of buyers default and units resell 10 percent lower, forfeited deposits cover the loss. If 25 percent default and units resell 20 percent lower, the gap exceeds the deposits by about 297,000. Deposits cushion a dip, not a crash, and my margin takes the rest.
terms: Qualifying sale — a pre-sale contract that meets the lender's definition, typically arm's length, outside rescission, with deposits paid and no unusual conditions.
Net proceeds — sale price less commissions, closing costs and taxes borne by the seller.
Pre-sale coverage — net proceeds of qualifying sales divided by the construction loan amount.

hostile.q: Your report says 92 sales. Why does your own schedule show only 77 qualifying?
hostile.a: Because I applied your definitions before you did. Four are related-party sales, six are inside the rescission period, three have an overdue second deposit and two carry a financing condition. On the 77, net proceeds are 32,571,000 against your 33,000,000 requirement, short by 429,000. The six rescission contracts qualify in a few days, so I expect to meet the threshold then, and I will send the updated schedule the day they do.

title: In the room: when the lender says your sales do not count
summary: A realistic meeting in which the lender's credit team rejects several of your pre-sales and delays the first draw. The lines to say, the lines never to say, the question behind the question, when to stay silent, and how to hold your state when your launch success is questioned.
body:
When a lender refuses to count some of your sales, it is not doubting your marketing; it is telling you which risks it will not take. Agree the definition, fix the sales that can be fixed, and replace the ones that cannot. Arguing that a weak sale is strong costs credibility you will need at completion.

Recall

Q. In the worked test, why did the pre-sales fall 429,000 short?

A. Because after removing non-qualifying contracts and deducting 6 percent of costs, net proceeds were 32,571,000 against a requirement of 33,000,000.

Q. What is a disclosure statement?

A. A document a developer gives a buyer describing the project, the unit, the budget, the risks and how deposits are protected.

Q. What is the walk-away number in a negotiation?

A. The least acceptable outcome, decided in writing before the meeting.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is the meeting that decides whether construction starts this month or in three months. The lender holds the decision, and you hold the evidence. A developer who arrives with a defence of every sale loses the meeting. A developer who arrives with the lender's own schedule already built, and a plan for each excluded sale, usually leaves with a date.

The scene

This is a composite example. You have 85 signed contracts on a hypothetical 120-unit building. Your marketing agent's report says the project is 71 percent sold. Ms Rahman, the lender's credit manager, and Mr Clarke, its counsel, have reviewed the file. Ms Rahman opens: "We count 70 qualifying sales. That is 58 percent. You need 65. The first draw is not available."

The lines to say

Begin by agreeing the frame: "I agree the test is qualifying sales on your definition, and I have run it myself. I also count 70 on a strict reading. I would like to go through the 15 we exclude, because I think five can qualify within two weeks and the rest need replacing." That is the most important sentence of the meeting. It tells her you are not going to fight her definition, which makes her willing to discuss its application.

Then group the exclusions. "Six are inside the rescission period; they qualify automatically on the 14th unless cancelled. Three have an overdue second deposit; our lawyer has issued notice and two have already paid since your report, here are the receipts. Four are bulk purchases by one investor; I accept you will not count more than two, and I will replace the other two. Two contain a financing condition; I will ask each buyer to waive it or I will replace them."

On the timeline: "If we reach 78 qualifying contracts by the 20th, will you confirm the first draw for the following week?" A specific number and a specific date convert a refusal into a conditional yes.

Say that out loud now.

The lines never to say

Never say "the market is hot, they will all close." Ms Rahman's job is to plan for the market that is not hot. Never say "the bulk buyer is a friend, I can vouch for him." A personal assurance about a buyer is exactly the concentration risk she excludes. Never suggest counting a related-party purchase "just for the threshold". That invites a question about whether the sale is genuine, and if a lender ever concludes a pre-sale was not genuine, the problem is no longer a delayed draw but a misrepresentation, which in most loans is an event of default and can reach you personally through a carve-out.

The question behind the question

When Mr Clarke asks "who is the bulk buyer and how is he funded?", he is asking whether that buyer will close if prices fall, and whether he could be a vehicle for something improper. Answer both: the buyer's identity, the deposit paid from his own account, and your compliance file on him. When Ms Rahman asks "how many contracts were signed in the last month?", she is asking whether demand is real and continuing, or whether the launch weekend was the peak. Answer with the weekly sales pace and the current price against the original list.

When to stay silent

When she states the exclusion count, do not dispute it immediately, even if you think one or two are arguable. Let the number sit, write it down, and then begin with agreement. When she says "we may need to revisit the loan amount", stay silent for a moment. She is testing whether you will offer a concession. You may not need to; the shortfall is a timing problem, and your plan addresses it.

How to hold your state

Hearing that your launch is less successful than your agent reported is uncomfortable, and the instinct is to defend the agent, the market and yourself. Separate the three. The agent's report counted contracts; the lender counts risk. Neither is wrong; they answer different questions. Arrive with your own qualifying schedule already built, so that nothing in her number is a surprise, and your composure follows from preparation rather than effort.

Reading the outcome

The worked result. On the 14th, five of the six rescission contracts hold and one cancels: 75 qualifying. Two overdue deposits are paid: 77. Two bulk purchases are accepted: 79. One financing condition is waived: 80. Eighty qualifying contracts out of 120 is about 67 percent, above the 65 percent threshold. Ms Rahman confirms the first draw for the 27th. The delay costs about two weeks of land carry, perhaps 75,000 dollars at a hypothetical 150,000 a month. Arguing the original 85 would have cost far more in credibility, and credibility is what you will draw on at completion, when the lender decides whether to extend a maturity while the last units close.

Notice what the second check shows. The lender's definition turned 85 contracts into 80 genuine ones. Those five missing contracts are the ones most likely to fail at completion. The lender's filter is also your best forecast of who will close.

After the meeting

Send Ms Rahman a written summary the same afternoon: the 70 counted, the 15 excluded grouped by reason, the plan and date for each group, and the condition agreed for the draw. Attach the deposit receipts. Then update your own qualifying schedule daily until the 20th, and send it to her each time it changes. A lender who receives the evidence before she asks for it begins to rely on your reporting, and that reliance is worth more at completion than any single concession won in the room. Finally, tell your marketing agent to report qualifying sales on the lender's definition from now on, so that the next report you read is the one the lender will read.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk in this room is defending a sale you know is weak, and in doing so making the lender doubt the strong ones. The control is to build the lender's schedule yourself, concede what does not qualify, and spend the meeting on a dated plan to replace it.

The beginner's mistake

The beginner quotes the marketing agent's percentage. Quote the qualifying percentage, on the lender's definition, every time.

Callback

In week 6 we practised hostile questions with acknowledge, bridge, answer, and a commitment to confirm by a date. "I agree with your count, here is how five more qualify, I will confirm by the 20th" is that pattern exactly, applied to the meeting that starts construction.

Recap

Agree the lender's definition first. Group the exclusions into those that qualify soon, those you can fix, and those you must replace. Ask for a conditional date tied to a number. Never vouch for a buyer or count a related-party sale. Treat the lender's filter as your own forecast of who will close.

Next: Kema closes the week with six questions, a Red Pen drill on a sales report, and a boardroom explanation of pre-sales.
checklist: Build the lender's qualifying schedule before the meeting
Open by agreeing the lender's definition
Group exclusions: qualifying soon, fixable, to replace
Bring receipts for any deposit paid since the lender's report
Ask for a conditional draw date tied to a qualifying number
Never vouch for a buyer or count a related-party sale
Answer the question behind each question with evidence
Report the qualifying percentage, never the agent's figure
head: Field checklist
speak: Mr Shabazz, the pre-sales meeting in one minute. The lender counts 70 qualifying sales out of my 85 contracts and says the first draw is not available. I open by agreeing her definition and saying I count 70 too. Then I group the 15 exclusions: six in rescission that qualify automatically on the 14th, three overdue deposits of which two have now paid, four bulk purchases of which she will count two, and two financing conditions I will ask buyers to waive. I ask for a conditional first draw date if we reach 78 by the 20th. I never vouch for a buyer and never ask her to count a related-party sale, because a sale that is not genuine is a misrepresentation. I stay silent when she mentions the loan amount. The result: 80 qualifying, about 67 percent, and a draw two weeks later for about 75,000 of carry.
terms: Bulk purchase — the purchase of several units in one project by a single buyer or related group, which lenders often limit when counting pre-sales.
Concentration risk — the risk that a large share of sales depends on one buyer or group, whose failure would hit many units at once.
Misrepresentation — a false statement of fact that induces a contract; in a loan it is typically an event of default.

hostile.q: Why should we count any of the bulk investor's four purchases?
hostile.a: You should count no more than your policy allows, and I accept two. He has paid full deposits from his own account, our compliance file on him is complete, and his contracts carry no assignment right before completion. I will replace the other two with individual buyers, and I am reporting the bulk purchases separately each month so you can see the concentration.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 41 review: condominium pre-sales
summary: Six questions on deposits, trust and escrow, deposit insurance, pre-sale thresholds and buyer default, a recap of the week, a Red Pen drill on a hypothetical weekly sales report with planted defects, and a two-minute boardroom explanation with a model answer.
body:
This week came down to one idea: pre-sales are evidence the building will be bought, and the buyers' money that comes with them is held for the buyers. Count only what the lender counts, keep every deposit where the law says, and stress the closings for the market that does not cooperate.

Recall

Q. What is concentration risk in pre-sales?

A. The risk that a large share of sales depends on one buyer or related group, whose failure would hit many units at once.

Q. What is the in-balance test?

A. A check that the undrawn loan plus committed equity is enough to finish the project, with any shortfall funded by the borrower before the next draw.

Q. What is a conditional purchase of land?

A. A binding contract that completes only if stated conditions, such as approvals or financing, are met by a date.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a review turns a week of ideas into a reflex. Answer each question aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. Who does a buyer's deposit belong to before completion? Answer: The buyer, held in trust or escrow under rules the purchase agreement cannot override, until completion or a release the law allows, typically against insurance or a bond.

Question 2. What makes a sale qualifying for a lender? Answer: Typically an arm's length buyer, outside the rescission period, with the required deposits paid and no unusual conditions such as a financing condition or a right to assign before completion.

Question 3. Why are released deposits not equity? Answer: Because they are owed back to buyers if the sale fails and are usually backed by the developer's indemnity to the insurer, so they behave like a conditional loan.

Question 4. What is a rescission period, and how does it affect a sales report? Answer: A short window in which a buyer may cancel without penalty. Sales inside it are provisional and should be reported separately from firm sales.

Question 5. In the worked test, when did deposits fail to cover buyer defaults? Answer: In the severe case, with 25 percent of buyers defaulting and units resold 20 percent lower, the resale gap exceeded the forfeited deposits by about 297,000.

Question 6. What is Rule 41? Answer: Buyers' deposits are never my working capital; they stay in trust or are released only against protection the law allows, and every build must be fully funded without any deposit I could be forced to return.

Say that out loud now.

Week recap

Day 1 set out deposit structures, trust, insurance, thresholds and buyer default. Day 2 took Evergrande apart and found buyers' money used as working capital. Day 3 priced the trade between price and pace, and the true nature of released deposits. Day 4 read trust rules, disclosure, cooling-off and forfeiture, and compared Canada and Guyana in concept. Day 5 filtered a sales report to qualifying net proceeds and stressed the closings. Day 6 agreed the lender's definition and replaced the sales that did not count.

Red Pen drill

Read this hypothetical weekly sales report and find the defects before reading on.

Weekly sales report. Units sold: 90 of 120, 75 percent, exceeding the lender's 65 percent threshold. Includes 12 contracts signed this weekend, and 5 units purchased by the developer's holding company to support momentum. Deposits received: 4,200,000, of which 1,000,000 has been applied to the design team's outstanding invoices on our second project pending release of that project's loan. Average price achieved: 465,000, above budget. Buyer default risk: nil, as all buyers have paid deposits. Recommend first draw request this week.

The defects. First, the 12 contracts signed this weekend are almost certainly inside any rescission period and are provisional. Second, the 5 units bought by the developer's own holding company are related-party sales that no lender will count and that raise questions about whether demand is genuine. Removing both, firm qualifying sales are at most 73 units, about 61 percent, below the threshold. Third, and most serious, applying 1,000,000 of deposits to another project's invoices is the Evergrande pattern in miniature and, in most deposit regimes, a breach of trust; it must be reversed and disclosed to the lender and counsel immediately. Fourth, the report quotes units, not net proceeds of qualifying sales, which is what the lender tests. Fifth, an average price above budget may be flattered by the related-party purchases, which could have been at any price. Sixth, buyer default risk is never nil: deposits cushion a moderate fall, not a severe one. Seventh, the recommendation to request the first draw this week rests on a threshold the project has not met.

Boardroom drill

Explain this week to a board in two minutes. Try it now, aloud, then compare with this model answer.

Model answer: "We have 92 signed contracts on a 120-unit building, and 77 qualify on the lender's definition after removing related-party, rescission, overdue-deposit and conditional sales. Net proceeds of those 77 are about 32,600,000 against a requirement of 33,000,000, and six contracts leaving their rescission period this week should close the gap. Deposits of 3,465,000 are held in our lawyer's trust account, reconciled weekly, and none has been released. The build is fully funded by the loan and our equity without relying on deposits. Our main risk is buyers failing to close in a falling market: deposits cover a 10 percent default with a 10 percent price fall, but not a 25 percent default with a 20 percent fall, so our contingency and margin are sized for that severe case."

Score yourself

Record your answer and score it 1 to 5 on four things. Accuracy: were the qualifying count and net proceeds right? Structure: did you open with qualifying sales against the threshold? Composure: steady pace and a pause after each key number? The hard question: did you say what happens in a severe default?

Where you will meet this again

In week 42 project finance asks the same question about every source of money: who bears the risk if the project fails. In week 44 the default stress becomes a full stress test with triggers. And in week 124 pre-sales return as a marketing, pricing and consumer protection discipline, including selling to buyers abroad.

A practice habit for the week ahead

Take any sales report you can find, real or hypothetical, and spend fifteen minutes on three tasks. Strike out every sale the lender would not count, and state why. Convert the rest to net proceeds and compare with a coverage requirement you choose. And trace every deposit to where it is held. If you cannot say, within a minute, where a particular buyer's deposit is sitting today, the report is not ready to send to anyone.

Then practise the boardroom answer twice more, once to a lender and once to an investor. The facts are the same; the order of emphasis is not. The lender wants qualifying coverage first; the investor wants the severe-case margin first.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is buyers' money used for anything the protocol does not allow. The control is separate project ledgers, trust accounts and a monthly reconciliation reported to the board.

The beginner's mistake

Quoting the agent's sold percentage instead of the lender's qualifying net proceeds.

Callback

In week 39 we learned that a construction lender funds only while its conditions are met. The pre-sale threshold is the condominium's version of that condition precedent: the one that decides whether the first draw happens at all.

Recap

Count qualifying sales on net proceeds, keep every deposit in trust until the law allows release, never pool project money, and stress closings for a severe default.

Next: Priya on project finance: special purpose vehicles, the recourse spectrum and what lenders control when they lend to a project rather than a person.

head: The six questions
speak: Mr Shabazz, week 41 in sixty seconds. A condominium is repaid by closings, so the lender needs pre-sales before it funds. Buyers pay staged deposits that belong to them, held in trust until the law allows release, often against insurance. Evergrande showed what happens when buyers' money becomes working capital, giving Rule 41: deposits are never my working capital, and every build is fully funded without them. Released deposits are a conditional loan backed by my indemnity, not equity. A launch discount is worth it only if the speed saves more. Trust rules override the contract, sales in a rescission period are provisional, and a reasonable deposit may be kept on default. The lender counts qualifying net proceeds, so 92 contracts became 77. Deposits cushion a moderate default, not a severe one. And in the room I agree the lender's definition and replace the sales that do not count.
terms: Pre-sale threshold — the level of qualifying sales a lender requires before funding a condominium build.
Deposit trust — the holding of a buyer's deposit by a third party for the buyer until completion or permitted release.
Pre-sale coverage — net proceeds of qualifying sales divided by the construction loan.

hostile.q: Your report says 75 percent sold and recommends a draw this week. Is that true?
hostile.a: No, and I am withdrawing it. Twelve contracts are inside their rescission period and five are our own holding company's purchases; neither qualifies, which takes us to about 61 percent. A million dollars of deposits was applied to another project's invoices, which should never have happened; it is being restored to trust today and I am informing you and our counsel in writing. I will resubmit on qualifying net proceeds when we meet the threshold.
